One feature stands out: post_attention_layernorm in layers 4 and 6–10 has 41–64 dimensions with scale |1+w| < 0.1, while the median scale there is 1–10. Attention in those layers is effectively barred from writing those residual coordinates.

Next I will check whether those silenced dimensions are the same set across layers (a structured feature) and whether they coincide with the massive dimensions. I will also run two cheap weight scans for edit patterns my earlier scans could not see:
- **Projected-out direction:** a direction projected out of a matrix would leave a near-zero smallest singular value in the gate/up input space or the down output space.
- **Swapped or replaced neurons:** these would show up as outliers in the alignment between each neuron's gate row, up row and down column.

I will also check whether v0 is essentially a coordinate axis (natural massive-dimension reader) or a dense direction. A near-zero singular value or a cluster of alignment outliers would give a concrete edit candidate. A clean result would close the weight-anomaly line and move me to activation-based localization.

Results from the last block:
- **Silenced post-attention dimensions:** they mostly differ from layer to layer (Jaccard 0.2–0.5; only 11 shared by layers 7–10, none of them massive dimensions). That looks like ordinary learned sparsity, not one planted subspace.

- **No projected-out direction:** no MLP matrix has a near-zero singular value. Layer 4 is a mild oddity: its minimum singular values are about 0.1 of the median in all three matrices, against about 0.2 elsewhere.
- **No swapped MLP layers:** the gate/up/down alignment statistics vary smoothly across layers.

Sabotage that keeps norms intact can still hide in attention: a head's query block or output block swapped in from another layer, or scrambled. A trained head's query rows should match its own layer's k_proj better than other layers' k_proj, and its output block should match its own layer's v_proj (a composition stronger than a random pairing). I will compute, for every head, the normalised QK and OV alignment against the k_proj and v_proj of all 26 layers. A head whose best match is another layer, or that is no better than random with its own layer, would be a concrete swap candidate. A clean diagonal for all 104 heads closes this line.

K14 is not scrambled. Like K13 and K15, it matches the query heads of layers 7–16 at 1.2–1.35. Its spectrum is heavy-tailed (s1/median 5.9), and its rows keep a strong RoPE pair structure (+0.60), as do layer 14's query heads (+0.69, the highest of any layer). The low self-alignment of layer 14 is therefore best explained by mostly positional (RoPE-driven) heads, whose queries and keys share little content subspace. I am closing the attention-swap line.

Taken together, the weight-only scans have found one planted-looking structure, the v0 group. Removing it did not help.
